MUJAHID:v2p762/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p762/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p762/r1.claim: Mujahid says the sun's duha is its light.

FARRA:v3p266/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p266/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p266/r1.claim: Ḍuḥāhā means its daylight, and al-ḍuḥā likewise means the entire day.

FARRA:v3p266/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p266/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p266/r2.claim: The kasra in rhyming forms from wāw roots follows the yāʾ-based pattern begun in the sūra; a sequence beginning in wāw could instead take fatḥa throughout.

FARRA:v3p266/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p266/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p266/r3.claim: Ḥamza's opening of wāw-derived forms while keeping kasra on yāʾ forms shows poor grasp of Arabic patterns; with wāw alone he prefers fatḥa, while yāʾ permits either vowel.

TAB-FULL:v24p434#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p434#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p434#2/r1.claim: God swears by the sun and its daytime; its manifest light is the day.

TAB-FULL:v24p434#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p434#2/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p434#2/r2.claim: Qatadah takes the sun's ḍuḥā as the whole daytime.

TAB-FULL:v24p434#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p434#2/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v24p434#2/r3.claim: Mujahid glosses the sun's ḍuḥā as its light.

ZAJJAJ:v5p331/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p331/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p331/r1.claim: The oath’s answer is “the one who purifies it succeeds,” meaning “has indeed succeeded”; the long intervening speech replaces the omitted lām.

ZAJJAJ:v5p331/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p331/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p331/r2.claim: Ḍuḥāhā means the sun’s light; another view takes it as daytime.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r1.claim: Mujahid glosses the sun's brightness as its light or radiance.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r12.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r12.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r12.claim: Qatadah identifies the sun with daytime, the moon as following the new moon at its setting, and daylight as covering the sun.

NAHHAS:v5p235/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p235/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p235/r1.claim: In ordinary Arabic ḍuḥā is the sun's first rising and brightening; Mujāhid and al-Farrāʾ instead call it the daytime.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r1.speaker: ابن كثير وعاصم وابن عامر
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r1.claim: Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir open the endings in this sūrah, al-Layl, and al-Ḍuḥā.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r2.speaker: الكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r2.claim: Al-Kisāʾī uses imālah throughout these endings and the endings of al-Layl and al-Ḍuḥā.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r3.speaker: حمزة
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r3.claim: Ḥamzah varies the endings: he inclines ḍuḥāhā but opens talāhā and ṭaḥāhā, while inclining the remaining forms, including sajā and daḥāhā.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r4.speaker: نافع
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r4.claim: Nāfiʿ has several transmissions: some make the endings intermediate, while Warsh and Qālūn are also reported to open them all; another report opens only talāhā and inclines the rest.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r5.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r5.speaker: أبو عمرو
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r5.claim: Abū ʿAmr is reported as using intermediate imālah, while ʿAbbās reports fully inclined forms for selected endings; other transmissions describe his treatment across verse endings.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r6.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r6.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r6.claim: Imālah is licensed where the alif behaves as one originating in yāʾ, as in derived verbs and nouns; an alif from wāw, such as العصا, normally resists it.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r7.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r7.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r7.claim: Rare inclined examples with an alif from wāw are too uncommon to challenge the general pattern.

THALABI:v10p212#3/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p212#3/r1.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v10p212#3/r1.claim: He interprets the sun's brightness as its light.

THALABI:v10p212#3/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p212#3/r2.speaker: قتادة
THALABI:v10p212#3/r2.claim: He takes the sun's brightness as the whole daytime.

THALABI:v10p212#3/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p212#3/r3.speaker: مقاتل
THALABI:v10p212#3/r3.claim: He interprets it as the sun's heat, citing the verse about not suffering heat.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r1.claim: The opening makes two oaths, one by the sun and one by its brightness.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r2.claim: Mujahid explains the sun's duha as its radiance.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r3.speaker: اليزيدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r3.claim: Al-Yazidi takes duha to mean the sun's spreading out.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r4.speaker: السدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r4.claim: Al-Suddi interprets duha as the sun's heat.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r6.claim: Mawardi also allows that the oath concerns all creatures made visible by the sun.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281/r1.claim: Surat al-Shams is Meccan according to everyone.

QUSHAYRI:v3p424/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p424/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p424/r1.claim: The basmala speaks of God's eternal existence and enduring sublimity; spirits are stunned by majesty, while souls thirst for the kindness of beauty.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r1.claim: The sequence of oaths runs through qad aflaha, which is the answer to the oath.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r10.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r10.claim: The original sense of duha is sunlight; the time of sunrise was named from that light, which explains the light and whole-day interpretations.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r11.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r11.claim: The heat interpretation is the weakest, though it has a rationale because sunlight includes both brightness and heat.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r2.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r2.claim: The full answer is laqad aflaha, but the laam was omitted because the long passage of speech takes its place.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r3.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r3.claim: Ḍaḥw is the sun's rise in the day; ḍuḥā is a little later, and ḍiḥāʾ is the extended time near midday.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r4.speaker: أبو الهيثم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r4.claim: Duha is the time when the sun rises and its light becomes clear.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد والكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r5.claim: They take the sun's duha as its light.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r6.speaker: قتادة والفراء وابن قتيبة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r6.claim: They interpret duha as the whole day; al-Farra and Ibn Qutayba prefer this view.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r7.speaker: مقاتل وابن عباس عن عطاء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r7.claim: They interpret it as the sun's heat; al-Zajjaj mentions the light and whole-day views as well.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r8.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r8.claim: He derives ḍuḥā from ḍaḥ, the sun's light, proposing that the alif reflects earlier consonant changes.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r9.speaker: أبو الهيثم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p43#2/r9.claim: He argues that ḍaḥ is the opposite of shade, the sun's light on the ground, and derives it from ḍuḥā, opposite to al-Mubarrad's direction.

WAHIDI-QT:91:1/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:91:1/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:91:1/r1.claim: The sun's duha is its light.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:91:1-8/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:91:1-8/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:91:1-8/r1.claim: The sun's “morning brightness” means its light.

JISHUMI:v10p7429/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7429/r1.speaker: أبي
JISHUMI:v10p7429/r1.claim: A report from the Prophet says that reciting Sūrat al-Shams is like giving charity to everything reached by the sun and moon.

JISHUMI:v10p7429/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7429/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7429/r2.claim: The previous chapter describes success through obedience and punishment for corrupting oneself; this chapter calls obedience purification instead of the previous chapter's steep path, with the same meaning.

JISHUMI:v10p7429/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7429/r3.speaker: ابن كثير وابن عامر وعاصم
JISHUMI:v10p7429/r3.claim: They pronounce the verse endings with fatḥ and tafkhīm; al-Kisāʾī uses imāla throughout, while other readers use intermediate or root-conditioned patterns.

JISHUMI:v10p7429/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7429/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7429/r4.claim: Imāla lightens pronunciation; fatḥ is the original, while an intermediate sound both eases pronunciation and signals the original form.

JISHUMI:v10p7429/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7429/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7429/r5.claim: Ḍuḥā is the beginning of the sun's rising and of daytime; its root suggests appearing. The sacrifice term later extended to animals slaughtered after the opening period.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد والكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r1.claim: Mujahid and al-Kalbi say ضحاها is the sun’s light; dawn is when it rises and its light clears. Qatada says all daytime, Muqatil its heat.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r1.claim: ضحاها is the sun's light once it rises and its power appears; الضحوة is the day's rise, الضحى is later, and الضحاء is the extended day approaching midday.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.claim: The repeated wāws can govern both accusative and genitive: the oath-wāw omits its verb altogether and substitutes for it, while coordinated wāws inherit that double function, resolving the apparent two-governor problem.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r1.claim: God swears by the sun either to draw attention to it or by an implied phrase, by the sun.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r2.claim: Mujahid defines duha as the full rise and brightness of the sun.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r3.claim: Qatada takes duha to mean the whole daytime.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r4.speaker: مقاتل
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r4.claim: Muqatil interprets duha as the sun's heat, citing 20:119.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r5.claim: Duhāʾ with long ā means the period after that, extending until noon.

TABRISI:91:1-15/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:91:1-15/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:91:1-15/r1.claim: God may swear by created things to highlight their great value and benefit; the world's animals and plants depend on the sun's rising and setting.

TABRISI:91:1-15/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:91:1-15/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TABRISI:91:1-15/r2.claim: Duha is the sun's extended, spreading light; al-Kalbi shares this interpretation.

TABRISI:91:1-15/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:91:1-15/r3.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:91:1-15/r3.claim: Duha may mean the whole daytime.

TABRISI:91:1-15/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:91:1-15/r4.speaker: مقاتل
TABRISI:91:1-15/r4.claim: Duha may mean the sun's heat, as in the verse about not suffering heat in Ta Ha.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137/r1.speaker: مجاهد والزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137/r1.claim: Ḍuḥā can mean the sun's light; the term is also used for the clear light after sunrise.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137/r2.speaker: قتادة وابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137/r2.claim: Alternatively, ḍuḥā means the whole day.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137/r3.speaker: السدي ومقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137/r3.claim: Alternatively, it means the sun's heat.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.claim: The sura urges obedience and warns against disobedience; oaths by beneficial created things prompt reflection and gratitude because divine oaths weigh heavily on the heart.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r2.speaker: جماعة من أهل الأصول
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r2.claim: Some legal theorists supply 'Lord of' before the sun and other oath objects, understanding the oath to be by their Lord.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r4.speaker: القراء
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r4.claim: Readers vary between imala and full pronunciation in this sura's verse endings, sometimes applying imala throughout and sometimes only selectively.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r5.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r5.claim: Al-Farra explains imala in endings with roots from waw by their resemblance to words beginning with ya; forms such as tala and daha can shift toward ya in verbs.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r6.claim: Full non-imala is also sound because many Arabs do not incline these alifs toward ya, and letters that historically shifted from waw or ya do not always reveal the shift in pronunciation.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r7.claim: Hamza's mixed approach is also good: only alifs derived from ya warrant imala, while tala, daha and similar forms derive from waw.

RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r1.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r1.claim: Seven things are sworn by through 'successful indeed' as the oath's answer; al-Zajjaj says the lām of laqad is omitted because the long passage substitutes for it.

RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r2.speaker: مجاهد والكلبي
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r2.claim: Mujahid and al-Kalbi explain the sun's duha as its light.

RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r3.speaker: قتادة
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r3.claim: Qatada takes duha as the whole day, an interpretation preferred by al-Farra and Ibn Qutayba.

RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r4.speaker: مقاتل
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r4.claim: Muqatil interprets duha as the sun's heat; Razi considers this the weakest view because heat and light accompany one another.

RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r5.claim: The oath highlights the sun's benefits: sunrise awakens the world as if reviving the dead, and the growing life of day culminates at noon, analogous to the people of Paradise settling in their home.

RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.speaker: القفال
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.claim: Al-Qaffal says all four oaths are really about the sun through its midday light, the moon's borrowing its light, its emergence in daytime and its concealment at night.

RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r3.claim: Reflecting on the sun's finite size and composite parts reveals its createdness and leads the mind to the Creator's greatness.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r1.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r1.claim: Ḍuḥāhā means the sun's light and radiance; this is the second oath, and the term is attached to the sun because it comes when the sun rises.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r10.claim: Those who define it as all daylight do so because the sun's light persists; those who define it as light or heat treat them as inseparable.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r11.speaker: المبرد وأبو الهيثم
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r11.claim: They give competing etymologies: ḍuḥā derives from ḍaḥ, sunlight opposite shade, with the final letter shifted in pronunciation.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r2.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r2.claim: He interprets the term as the sun's splendor.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r3.speaker: السدي
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r3.claim: He interprets it as the sun's heat.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r4.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r4.claim: He says God placed both light and heat in the sun.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r5.speaker: اليزيدي
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r5.claim: He glosses ḍuḥāhā as the sun's spreading or extension.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r6.speaker: الماوردي
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r6.claim: Another view takes it as all creatures on earth made visible by the sun, so the oath includes them.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r7.claim: Ḍuḥā is usually feminine, though it can be masculine; grammarians connect it either to the plural of ḍaḥwah or to a noun-pattern like ṣurad.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r8.claim: The word is an indeclinable time adverb in phrases such as 'I met him this morning.'

QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r9.speaker: الفراء وقتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:91:1/r9.claim: They use ḍuḥā for the whole day, while common Arabic usage means sunrise and the period shortly afterward; extended brightness is ḍuḥāʾ.

BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r1.claim: الضحى is sunlight at sunrise; ضحوة is earlier than ضحى, while ضحاء is the extended day near noon.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#4/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#4/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#4/r1.claim: The sun's duha is its light when it rises and its power becomes manifest.

QASHANI:91:1-3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:91:1-3/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:91:1-3/r1.claim: The sun is the spirit and its light spreading through the body and shining upon the self.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.claim: The Meccan surah swears by parts of the upper and lower worlds and by the soul as an instrument of reflection; it moves from disbelievers' afterlife to their worldly destruction and eventual Fire.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r8.claim: The discussion of ḍuḥā was previously given under the verse about people gathering at that time in Sūrat Ṭā Hā.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r1.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r1.claim: Mujahid defines ḍuḥā as the rising and full development of light.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r2.speaker: مقاتل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r2.claim: Muqatil interprets ḍuḥā as the sun's heat, taking the consequence for the word itself.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r3.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r3.claim: Qatada says ḍuḥā is the entire daytime, but the author rejects this because the surah separately swears by the day.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r4.claim: In standard Arabic ḍuḥā is shortly after sunrise; the longer ḍuḥāʾ lasts toward noon.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r5.claim: The author doubts the report that al-Mubarrad derived ḍuḥā from ḍaḥ, since the two are separate roots and al-Mubarrad would not make that claim.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.claim: For eloquence, all the pronouns through يغشاها should refer to the sun; this matches the preceding description of day revealing it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.speaker: القفال
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.claim: Al-Qaffāl summarizes the oaths as four solar aspects: daytime brightness and activity, the moon taking its light, full appearance, and disappearance at night.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.speaker: أصحابنا
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.claim: The author's colleagues interpret سبحان من سخركن as a proper name, with mā infinitival and temporal.

SAMIN-DURR:91:1/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:1/r1.speaker: المبرد
SAMIN-DURR:91:1/r1.claim: Al-Mubarrad is quoted as deriving duha and dawha from dhaw (‘light’), with alif and wāw replacing the letter ḥā’; the author calls this nearly fabricated despite the scholar’s standing.

IBNKATHIR:91:1/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:1/r2.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
IBNKATHIR:91:1/r2.claim: A report in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections says the Prophet asked Muʿādh why he had not prayed with al-Aʿlā, al-Shams, or al-Layl.

IBNKATHIR:91:1/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:1/r4.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR:91:1/r4.claim: Alternatively, ḍuḥāhā is the whole day.

IBNKATHIR:91:1/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:1/r5.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR:91:1/r5.claim: God swears by the sun and its day: the sun's visible light is daytime.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r1.claim: The sura follows the claim that humanity is in hardship and ends with the sealed fire: God is the ultimate agent who turns between a person, heart, and intellect and guides or misguides souls.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r2.claim: The oath begins with the heavenly realm and then souls to establish God’s knowledge, power, necessary existence, and attributes, prompting gratitude as the highest practical perfection.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r3.claim: The sun brings benefit and harm through light and heat, like intellects that illuminate when sound and become dark when corrupted.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r4.claim: Ḍuḥā is the sun’s light from its remarkable body and recalls fires as its power rises; ḍuḥā also means the morning after sunrise, while ḍuḥāʾ means intense heat after a long day.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#s091/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#s091/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#s091/r1.claim: The purpose of Surat al-Shams is to show God’s control of souls, the lamps of bodies, guiding them to happiness or misery just as He controls the sun and all creation.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#s091/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#s091/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#s091/r2.claim: The sura’s name points to its subject through reflection on the oath and what is sworn by.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#s091/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#s091/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#s091/r3.claim: The basmala names God as supreme king with general control, merciful to all, and especially guiding whom He wills to complete their blessing.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437/r1.claim: The purpose of Surat al-Shams is to show God’s control of souls, the lamps of bodies, guiding them to happiness or misery just as He controls the sun and all creation.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437/r2.claim: The sura’s name points to its subject through reflection on the oath and what is sworn by.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437/r3.claim: The basmala names God as supreme king with general control, merciful to all, and especially guiding whom He wills to complete their blessing.

DURR-FULL:v8p497/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p497/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p497/r2.claim: The Prophet rebuked Muadh for overlong prayer and directed him to recite shorter chapters, including the chapters beginning with glorification, the sun, dawn, and night.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r1.claim: The surah is Meccan and has fifteen verses.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r2.claim: He said the surah was revealed in Mecca.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r3.speaker: ابن الزبير
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r3.claim: He likewise said the surah was revealed in Mecca.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r4.speaker: بريدة
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r4.claim: The Prophet recited this surah and similar short surahs in the night prayer.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r5.claim: The Prophet told him to recite both the Night and the Sun surahs in the dawn prayer.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r6.speaker: عقبة بن عامر
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r6.claim: The Prophet instructed them to pray the two midmorning rakʿahs using the Sun and Midmorning surahs.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r7.speaker: النعمان بن بشير
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r7.claim: He said the Prophet recited al-Aʿla and the Sun surah in the two Eid prayers.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.claim: He glossed the sun as its light, the moon as following it, daylight as illuminating it, God as builder of heaven, the earth as spread out, inspiration as showing good and evil, and corruption as leading astray.

BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r1.claim: The sun's duha is its spreading light when it rises, its power becomes manifest, and its radiance extends over the earth.

BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r2.claim: In the inward reading, the sun is the spirit and its light spreads through the body and shines upon the self.

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.claim: Although the conditional sense of idha seems to require an answer and an operator, the author reads it causally in these oaths: swear because the moon follows, the day reveals, and the night covers; al-Qamus also allows a present-time meaning, “when.”

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.claim: The oath wa's are conjunctive and share the implied verb, avoiding the problem of coordinating words governed by different agents or multiplying oaths with one answer.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r1.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas, authenticated by al-Hakim, explains duha as the sun's light when it has risen and its dominion appears.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r2.claim: Strictly, duha is when the sun moves visibly away from the eastern horizon; its successive times are called dhuwa, duha, then extended duhaʾ. Attributed to the sun, it figuratively means its shining.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r3.speaker: المبرد
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r3.claim: Al-Mubarrad reportedly derives duha from ḍaḥḥ, the sun's light, and treats the alif and wāw in related forms as reversed from a second ḥāʾ.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r4.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r4.claim: Abu Hayyan suspects that this derivation was falsely attributed to al-Mubarrad, since the two forms have different roots and one is not derived from the other.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r5.claim: A reply says the claim was not about small-scale derivation; Alusi remarks that even a novice knows the difference.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r6.speaker: مقاتل
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140/r6.claim: Muqatil explains duha as the sun's heat, by reference to its necessary effect; he also says it means the whole day, which Alusi considers a remote interpretation for this oath.

ELMALILI:91:1/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:1/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:1/r1.claim: Duha literally describes the sun rising above the visible horizon and its light spreading; by extension it names the morning period, with dahwa, duha, and daha marking successively later hours.

ELMALILI:91:1/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:1/r2.speaker: müfessirîn
ELMALILI:91:1/r2.claim: Because the word is attached to the sun, exegetes interpret its duha as the sun’s radiance as it shines.

ELMALILI:91:1/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:1/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:1/r3.claim: The oath first invokes the sun in all its properties and then especially its light when it appears.

ELMALILI:91:1/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:1/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:1/r4.claim: The sun drives major movements and transformations in the celestial system and life, both at rising and setting; its light makes the physical world visible and reveals its Creator’s care and power.

ELMALILI:91:1/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:1/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:1/r5.claim: Heat and light are its clearest benefits; both are felt especially at duha, and the sun’s heat connects to the preceding surah’s fire while light is what first strikes the eye.

ELMALILI:91:1/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:1/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:1/r6.claim: Light presents external forms to conscious sight; through reflection between the world and the self, together with other senses, it develops spiritual understanding and guides recognition of God.

ELMALILI:91:1/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:1/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:1/r7.claim: This illumination can lead purified souls to return contentedly to God and attain success under the call to enter among His servants and Paradise.

ELMALILI:91:1/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:1/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:1/r8.claim: Light becomes fully meaningful in conscious perception, joining external and internal experience; it models how awareness links people to what lies beyond them, while creatures without consciousness have no concept of sun or light.

ELMALILI:91:1/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:1/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:1/r9.claim: The wording draws attention to the sun’s illuminating and guiding role, then moves through changing light and darkness, the heavens and earth, and the soul’s inspired good and evil toward purification and success.

QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r1.claim: This short Meccan surah’s unified rhyme and rhythm frame its central truth: the human soul’s innate capacities, the person’s role in shaping it, and responsibility for its destiny; the Thamud story models failure to purify it.

QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r2.claim: God’s oath gives cosmic scenes and the soul special worth and invites reflection on their meaning; creation and the human heart communicate through an innate, wordless spiritual language.

QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r3.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r3.speaker: قول مروي
QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r3.claim: A reported interpretation takes al-duha to mean the entire daytime.

QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r4.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r4.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:91:1/r4.claim: He sees no need to leave the nearby, specific meaning of the bright morning hours, whose distinctive quality carries its own significance.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r1.claim: The surah is usually called al-Shams; al-Bukhārī's title quotes its first verse, a name preferred to prevent confusion with al-Takwīr, and al-Itqān does not list it among surahs with multiple names.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r2.claim: The surah is Meccan by agreement, twenty-sixth in revelation after al-Qadr and before al-Burūj; most regions count fifteen verses, while Meccans count sixteen.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r3.claim: The surah warns idolaters that they may soon suffer the punishment that struck Thamūd for shirk and defiance of their messenger.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p365/r4.claim: Its majestic oaths draw evidence of God's unique divinity from the artistry of the sun, moon, heavens, earth, and the soul's paths toward guidance or ruin.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.claim: The oath confirms the threat of destruction implicitly conveyed by the news; each waw following a pause is an oath particle, and the sun, moon, sky, earth, and human soul display God's wise and powerful creation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.claim: The dawn brightness, moon following the sun, daylight, and night are all examples of the fine order God established.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r3.claim: Ḍuḥā is when the sun rises above the eastern horizon and its rays appear, at roughly the height that looks like a spear's length.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r4.claim: The oath is prepared by noting that purifying the soul leads to success, while neglecting its reform leads to immorality and loss.

TABATABAI:91:1-8/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:91:1-8/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:91:1-8/r2.claim: Duha is the sun's spreading and the day's extension, and the time takes its name from that; the oath is by the sun and its light spread over earth.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.claim: Qur'anic oaths probably draw on a characteristic expression of pre-Islamic soothsayers, though the connection remains insufficiently researched.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.claim: The structure and function of cumulative oath series are discussed at 93:1–2, with many parallels.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.claim: An eight-verse oath series leads into the antithetical statement in verses 9–10; the pre-Islamic genre is repurposed in verses 5–7 to express biblical creation ideas.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.claim: The series moves through three complementary or contrasting pairs—sun/moon, night/day, heaven/earth—then the soul, whose opposed moral capacities are specified in verse 8.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.claim: The oath series narrows from cosmic creation, traced vertically from celestial bodies to earth, to the human moral subject.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.claim: Its shift from creation to humanity resembles the 81:1–14 sequence, which evokes the world's eschatological dissolution rather than cyclical operation.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.claim: A caesura after verse 4 divides effects and activities of the oath's objects in verses 1–4 from references to God's creating activity in verses 5–8.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r1.claim: Wa-ḍuḥāhā literally means the sun's bright morning and belongs to a broader set of oaths about times of day and night.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.claim: The translation signals paired oaths by beginning verses 2, 4, and 6 with and, following Neuwirth.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.claim: One might translate talā as the moon falling behind the sun, but the parallel between verses 1–3 and 2–4 favors the moon's following the day into night.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r1.claim: Balad warned Quraysh that Makkah’s prosperity came through Abraham’s prayer and the House, so they must not become arrogant; Shams warns what follows if they persist.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.claim: The world appears to contain opposing forces, yet God keeps them within limits and in harmony; their accord preserves the universe.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.claim: The sun, moon, day, and night are complementary phenomena; their apparent oppositions in appearance, temperament, and effects serve in harmony.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.claim: Earlier sūrahs used this complementarity for arguments about monotheism and the Day of Judgement; here the focus is how the apparent opposites work together.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.claim: The cosmic order prevents the sun or moon from intruding on the other’s appointed time and keeps day and night within their roles, as 36:40 says.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.claim: Harmony among opposites sustains the universe; their obedience to limits teaches people to stay within God’s bounds, since exceeding them creates disorder God will not tolerate.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.claim: Some take 91:9–10 as the oath’s complement; Islahi gives weight to al-Zamakhsharī’s rejection of that view.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.claim: The sun, moon, day, and night show that a powerful, self-sustaining God keeps the world’s elements on their appointed paths, preventing their collision from destroying it.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.claim: Suppressing the complement lets everything evident from the oaths count as its content; one prominent implication is that God destroys rebellious nations.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.claim: Oaths by natural phenomena highlight cosmic order and its benefits, the Creator's power, and the importance of what follows.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r2.speaker: Müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r2.claim: Duha-ha, translated “morning brightness,” has also been read as the sun's light, brightness, morning time, or daytime.

STUDYQURAN:91:1/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:1/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:91:1/r1.claim: For the meaning of ḍuḥāhā, translated “morning brightness,” consult the introduction to Sūrah 93.

STUDYQURAN:91:intro/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:intro/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:91:intro/r1.claim: Al-Shams is early Makkan and thought to follow Sūrah 97; it takes its title from the opening oath.

STUDYQURAN:91:intro/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:intro/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:91:intro/r2.claim: The first ten verses establish physical and spiritual polarity: eight oaths lead to the soul's choice between iniquity and purity, continuing 90:10's two highways and right-left contrast.
